warmup.q: A service holding 512 MB in memory calls fork to start a child. Right after fork returns, about how much extra RAM does the machine use?
options: About 512 MB: the child gets its own copy of every page
About 1 MB, for the child's page table; the 512 MB stays shared until one side writes
Nothing at all: the child even shares the parent's page table
256 MB: the kernel splits the pages between the two
warmup.why: On Linux fork copies the page table, not the pages. In the lab box the child of a 512 MB process was running 1.7 ms after fork with Shared 512 MB and Private 0 in smaps_rollup. Each process needs its own page table, so the child can't share the parent's, and the kernel copies a page only when one side first writes to it.

sections.h: fork shares every page, and the first write copies it
sections.html:
cow.c fills 512 MB of memory and then calls fork. The child is running 1.7 ms later. Copying the same 512 MB with memcpy takes 33 ms in the lab box, and needs a second 512 MB of RAM to copy into. Lesson 2 of this track said the child starts as a copy of the parent, and promised a trick that makes the copy cheap. This is the trick.

Start with the simplest version that would work: at fork, the kernel copies every page of the parent into fresh frames (a frame is a 4 KB piece of physical RAM, from lesson 6). It's correct, and it's slow exactly where it hurts. A 4 GB JVM that starts a helper with fork and exec copies 4 GB, and exec throws it all away a millisecond later. A Redis server holding 10 GB forks a child to write a snapshot to disk. The child only reads, yet copying would need 20 GB.

The next try shares instead of copying. The kernel gives the child its own page table (the per-process map from virtual pages to frames, lesson 6), and its entries point at the parent's frames. That costs only the table: about 1 MB of entries for 512 MB of 4 KB pages. But now a write by the parent would change the child's memory too, and the child was promised its own copy.

The last piece is the permission bits in each entry. At fork the kernel marks every entry read-only, in the parent and in the child. Reads work as before. The first write to a page, by either side, isn't allowed, so the CPU raises a page fault (the exception that hands control to the kernel, lesson 6). The kernel's fault handler sees that the region is writable and the frame is shared. It copies that one 4 KB page into a new frame, points the writer's entry at the copy, makes it writable and restarts the store. This is copy-on-write. The kernel counts the entries that point at each frame, and when only one is left, a write fault just makes that entry writable again. The stepper walks through it.

/proc/<pid>/smaps_rollup shows the result. Shared counts pages whose frame another process maps too, Private counts pages only this process maps, and PSS (proportional set size) splits each shared page among its sharers. Right after fork the child has Shared 512 MB, Private 0 and Pss 256 MB. After it writes one byte in every fourth page, the kernel has made 32,768 copies (128 MB) at 1.6 to 1.9 µs each, and the child shows Shared 384 MB and Private 128 MB. RSS says 513 MB for each process the whole time, so adding up RSS would claim 1 GB. The two use 640 MB, and their PSS values add up to that.

Copy-on-write isn't free. Writing every page took the child 180 ms of faults, several times the memcpy. It wins because most children write a little, or call exec and write nothing.

stepper.title: fork, then one write
stepper.intro: Two page tables on top, RAM below. Each entry names the frame it points at and whether a write may go straight through; each frame shows how many entries point at it.

frames.say: fork builds the child a page table whose entries point at the parent's frames, and marks every entry read-only, the parent's too. Each frame now has two references. No data moved: the cost is the new page table, about 1 MB for 512 MB of memory.

try.expect:
Timings change from run to run:

copying 512 MB with memcpy: 33 ms
parent before fork     Rss  513 MB  Pss  512 MB  Shared    0 MB  Private  512 MB
fork returned in the child after 1.7 ms
child after fork       Rss  513 MB  Pss  256 MB  Shared  512 MB  Private    0 MB
child wrote to 32768 of 131072 pages: 32768 page faults in 58 ms (1.76 us each)
child after writes     Rss  513 MB  Pss  320 MB  Shared  384 MB  Private  128 MB

copying 512 MB with memcpy: 28 ms
...

child after writes     Rss  513 MB  Pss  512 MB  Shared    0 MB  Private  512 MB
...

One fault per page written, and each fault is one 4 KB copy. Rss never moves, because RSS counts shared pages in full in every process. Pss is the honest share: 256 MB each while everything is shared. When the child exits, the parent's pages are private again. Writing everything cost 180 ms in faults against 28 ms for one big memcpy: copy-on-write pays per page, and it wins only because most children write little.

video.title: Copy-on-write, overcommit and the OOM killer

sections.h: mmap can fill a region from a file instead of zeros
sections.html:
MapFile maps a 256 MB file with FileChannel.map and reads one byte from every page. The process's RssFile goes from 22 MB to 278 MB. RssAnon doesn't move.

Every region so far has been anonymous memory: it belongs to no file, and its pages start as zeros. The heap, thread stacks and the Java heap are all anonymous. The other kind of region is backed by a file. To see why it exists, look at how a program normally reads a file. The kernel keeps file data in RAM in the page cache (its in-memory copy of file pages, the subject of lesson 9 of this track). read() is a system call (lesson 1) that copies bytes from the page cache into the program's buffer. For a 2 GB index that a fraud check probes at random, that's a system call and a copy for every probe, and the hot pages sit in RAM twice.

mmap of a file removes both costs. The kernel records a region whose backing is the file. The first touch of a page faults, as in lesson 6, but this time the handler doesn't zero a frame. It finds the page cache frame that holds that part of the file, reading it from disk first if it isn't cached (a major fault), and points the entry at it. After that a probe is a plain memory load. Every process that maps the file points at the same frames, and those frames count as RssFile.

A file mapping is either shared or private. With MAP_SHARED, a write goes into the page cache frame itself, so the file changes, every other process mapping it sees the change, and the kernel writes it to disk later. With MAP_PRIVATE, the entries start read-only and the first write is a copy-on-write fault, exactly as after fork: the writer gets an anonymous copy of that page, and the file never changes. This is how every process loads libc.so. Its code is mapped private, so a hundred processes share one copy of it in RAM.

The difference matters when memory runs short. The kernel can drop a clean file page at any moment, because it can read it back from the file. An anonymous page has no file to come back from, so the kernel can only move it to swap (disk space set aside for evicted anonymous pages), if the machine has any.

In Java, FileChannel.map returns a MappedByteBuffer. MapMode.READ_ONLY and MapMode.READ_WRITE give shared mappings, and MapMode.PRIVATE gives the copy-on-write one. Kafka maps its index files this way.

steps: MapFile writes a 256 MB file in /tmp, maps it read-only, reads one byte per page and prints the process's RssAnon and RssFile at each step. Then it maps the first page twice, writes S through a shared mapping and P through a private one, and reads the file's first two bytes back with a plain read.
Predict RssFile after the reads, and which of the two letters reaches the file.
Run it in the lab box. It deletes the file at the end.

code.title: in the lab box
code.html: javac -d /tmp/out os/src/demo/java/sfz/os/l07/demo/MapFile.java java -cp /tmp/out sfz.os.l07.demo.MapFile

try.expect:
before map     RssAnon   23 MB   RssFile   22 MB
after map      RssAnon   32 MB   RssFile   22 MB
after reading  RssAnon   33 MB   RssFile  278 MB
maps: ffff3c000000-ffff4c000000 r--s 00000000 00:ad 1336147                    /tmp/ledger.dat
file bytes 0-1: 'S' 0   private mapping sees 'S' 'P'

Mapping cost nothing; reading one byte per page brought 256 MB into RssFile, the page cache's frames for that file. The 9 MB that RssAnon gains at map is the JVM loading classes, not the file. In /proc/self/maps the region is r--s: readable and shared. The file got the shared S and not the private P. The private mapping still saw the S, because its page was copied only when it wrote the P, after the S was already there.

sections.h: The kernel promises more memory than it has
sections.html:
promise.c asks for 100 GB with mmap on the lab box's VM, which has 7.9 GB of RAM. The call returns at once. Asking for 1,000 GB works too.

That follows from lesson 6: mmap only records a region, and RAM arrives a page at a time on first touch. So the kernel has to decide how much to promise before it knows how much will be used. The simplest rule is honest bookkeeping: refuse any request that would push the total promised past RAM plus swap. It breaks on the first fork of a big process. A 4 GB JVM on an 8 GB machine forks a helper, the child is promised a private copy of all 4 GB, the total passes 8 GB, and fork fails, although copy-on-write would have copied a handful of pages before exec. The JVM's own habits break it too. It reserves its whole -Xmx heap at start-up, every thread reserves a 2 MB stack (lesson 3), and much of that is never touched.

So Linux overcommits: it promises more than it has and counts on most promises never being collected. /proc/meminfo keeps the books. Committed_AS is the total promised to all processes. CommitLimit is swap plus a share of RAM (vm.overcommit_ratio, 50% by default): here 1,024 MB of swap plus half of 7,935 MB, 4,991 MB. The setting vm.overcommit_memory picks the rule:

value rule
0 the default: refuse requests that obviously can't fit, say yes to the rest
1 always say yes
2 never let Committed_AS pass CommitLimit

The lab box's VM runs with 1, so Committed_AS reached 104,612 MB on a machine with 7,935 MB of RAM. Mode 2 sounds safer, and PostgreSQL's manual suggests it for database hosts, but on a busy machine fork and large reservations then fail with ENOMEM while plenty of RAM is still free.

The real cost of promising is where the failure lands. A refused mmap is an error code the program can handle. A broken promise shows up later, inside a page fault: the program is in the middle of an ordinary store instruction, and there's no call that could return an error. The kernel first tries to find a frame by reclaiming memory: it drops clean file pages, writes dirty ones back so it can drop them too, and moves anonymous pages to swap. If that can't free enough, there's one move left: kill a process and take its memory.

try.title: Ask for 100 GB and 1,000 GB

Predict whether 100 GB and 1,000 GB succeed on a VM with 8 GB, and how far Committed_AS moves. Then run it in the lab box.

code.title: in the lab box
code.html: gcc -O2 -o /tmp/promise os/c/l07/promise.c /tmp/promise 100 0 /tmp/promise 1000 0

try.expect:
vm.overcommit_memory = 1
before mmap      CommitLimit   4991 MB   Committed_AS    2212 MB   MemTotal  7935 MB
mmap of 100 GB returned 0xffe69de00000
after mmap       CommitLimit   4991 MB   Committed_AS  104612 MB   MemTotal  7935 MB
vm.overcommit_memory = 1

mmap of 1000 GB returned 0xff05b7c00000
after mmap       CommitLimit   4991 MB   Committed_AS 1026212 MB   MemTotal  7935 MB

Both succeed. Committed_AS counts each promise in full, and mode 1 ignores CommitLimit, so the VM happily promises 1 TB. These numbers are for the whole Docker VM (other containers' promises are in the 2,212 MB), because /proc/meminfo is not limited to your container. Under the default mode 0, a single request this far beyond RAM plus swap would be refused as an obvious overcommit.

sections.h: When a promise can't be kept, the OOM killer picks a process
sections.html:
In a container limited to 256 MB, promise.c reserves 4 GB without complaint, touches 192 MB of it, and is gone: Killed, exit code 137, and the container's memory.events file says oom_kill 1.

A container's limit is a cgroup setting. A cgroup is a group of processes the kernel counts and limits together (lesson 12 of this track builds one by hand), and docker run --memory 256m writes 268435456 into the group's memory.max. The kernel charges every page that the group's processes bring into RAM to the group, anonymous pages and page cache pages alike. When a fault would push the charge past memory.max, the kernel reclaims inside the group first. If that fails it runs the OOM killer (out of memory) on the group's processes only. In memory.events, max counts the times the group hit its limit and oom_kill counts the processes killed. Without a limit, the same thing happens machine-wide once RAM and swap run out.

The killer picks by size, not by guilt. Each candidate gets a badness score: its RSS plus its swap plus its page tables, in pages, plus oom_score_adj (from -1000 to 1000) thousandths of the memory it's allowed. The highest score gets SIGKILL. A process set to -1000 is never picked. Kubernetes sets this value for you: -997 for containers in Guaranteed pods, 1000 for BestEffort ones. So the process that asked for the last page often isn't the one that dies. A 1 GB JVM next to a 50 MB shell script loses, whichever of them allocated last.

A JVM lives under two memory limits, and they fail in different ways. -Xmx is the JVM's own limit on the Java heap. When the heap is full and garbage collection can't free enough, the JVM throws java.lang.OutOfMemoryError: Java heap space. That's an ordinary exception: you get a stack trace, -XX:+HeapDumpOnOutOfMemoryError writes a heap dump, and your code decides what happens next. memory.max is the kernel's limit on everything the process has in RAM: the heap pages it has touched, plus metaspace, the code cache, thread stacks, GC structures and native buffers (lesson 8 of this track takes those apart). Cross it and the kernel sends SIGKILL, which the JVM can't catch. No exception, no heap dump, no shutdown hook. The container exits with 137, which is 128 plus signal 9 (lesson 2).

Hog holds on to 1 MB arrays until something stops it. In the 256 MB container with no -Xmx, the JVM gave itself a 121 MB heap, and the heap filled first: OutOfMemoryError. With -Xmx1g the heap could outgrow the container, and the kernel killed the JVM at about 224 MB.

try.title: Get killed by the kernel, then by the JVM

MemTotal still says 7,935 MB inside a 256 MB container: /proc/meminfo shows the whole VM, and the limit lives in /sys/fs/cgroup/memory.max. The C program died at a store, 137 and one oom_kill. The JVM with its own 121 MB heap stopped itself with an exception and exit code 1, and oom_kill didn't move. With -Xmx1g there was no exception and no stack trace, only 137 and a second oom_kill. The max count (143 here) is how many times the group hit its limit and the kernel had to reclaim; it varies between runs.

refs.title: Control Group v2: memory.max and memory.events
Kubernetes: node out of memory behavior and oom_score_adj

analogy: Overcommit is an airline that sells 220 tickets for a 200-seat plane, because some passengers never show up. Copy-on-write is two travellers on one booking who share every detail until one of them changes a seat, and only that seat gets a new record. Most days nobody notices. On the day all 220 turn up, someone has to leave the plane, and the OOM killer is the gate agent who picks the passenger with the most luggage, whoever arrived last. The analogy breaks at the moment of choice. An airline asks for volunteers before boarding and pays them. The kernel finds out mid-flight, at a page fault in the middle of a store instruction, and removes the passenger with SIGKILL, without asking and without letting them pack.
world: A Quarkus payments service in a pod with a 1 GiB limit and -Xmx900m runs fine through testing and then restarts at peak with OOMKilled and exit code 137 in kubectl describe pod, with no OutOfMemoryError in the log and no heap dump. The heap never filled. The heap plus metaspace, thread stacks, Netty's direct buffers and malloc's arenas crossed 1 GiB, and the kernel killed the JVM. The fix is headroom: size the heap well under the limit and measure the rest (lesson 8). Copy-on-write shows up in the Redis your services call: BGSAVE forks, and a write-heavy minute during the snapshot copies pages until RSS nearly doubles, which in a tight container kills one of the two processes. And Kafka's brokers lean on file mappings: their index files are mmaped, so after a restart the first lookups take major faults until the page cache is warm.
mistake: Sizing -Xmx to the container limit, or setting -XX:MaxRAMPercentage=100. It feels like using the memory you pay for. But the heap is only part of what the kernel counts: metaspace, the code cache, every thread's stack, GC bookkeeping and native buffers come on top, and the kernel kills at memory.max with SIGKILL. You get no OutOfMemoryError, so -XX:+HeapDumpOnOutOfMemoryError never fires, and the next move, raising -Xmx, makes it worse. Read the kill from outside instead: exit code 137, OOMKilled in docker inspect or kubectl describe, and oom_kill in the container's memory.events. Then leave real headroom: a heap of about half to three quarters of the limit, checked against the JVM's actual RSS under load.

With a heap bigger than the container, the kernel's memory controller notices first, and its only tool is SIGKILL: the last line printed is whatever happened to be flushed. The left run is the one you want in production, which is why the heap must be smaller than the limit by more than the JVM's non-heap memory.

worked.title: Find out why a container exited with 137

steps.say: Start from the exit code. 137 is 128 + 9: the process got SIGKILL. Docker records whether the kernel's OOM killer sent it. (Kubernetes shows the same as Reason: OOMKilled under Last State in kubectl describe pod.)
steps.code: docker inspect -f 'ExitCode={{.State.ExitCode}} OOMKilled={{.State.OOMKilled}}' sfz-os07-oom # ExitCode=137 OOMKilled=true

steps.say: Confirm it from the cgroup. oom_kill counts processes the OOM killer took from this group; max counts how often the group hit memory.max. A growing max with no kills means the kernel is reclaiming hard to stay under the limit.
steps.code: cat /sys/fs/cgroup/memory.events # low 0 # high 0 # max 45 # oom 1 # oom_kill 1 # oom_group_kill 0

steps.say: Check what the JVM believes. -XshowSettings:system prints the limits it read from the cgroup, and MaxHeapSize is the heap it chose. In a 256 MB box with no flags, the JVM took 126 MB for the heap.
steps.code: java -XshowSettings:system -version 2>&1 | grep Memory # Memory Limit: 256.00M # Memory Soft Limit: 0.00K # Memory & Swap Limit: 256.00M java -XX:+PrintFlagsFinal -version 2>/dev/null | grep ' MaxHeapSize ' # size_t MaxHeapSize = 132120576 {product} {ergonomic}

steps.say: Decide which limit to move. If the log shows OutOfMemoryError, the heap was too small or something leaks on it. If it shows nothing and the exit was 137, heap plus non-heap crossed memory.max: lower the heap or raise the limit, and measure the non-heap part with NMT (lesson 8).
steps.code:
# heap too small:   OutOfMemoryError in the log, exit 1, oom_kill unchanged
# limit too small:  nothing in the log, exit 137, oom_kill + 1

lab.title: Build a copy-on-write memory model with an OOM killer
steps: Open cow-512m.txt: a real run of cow.c in the lab box. One test replays it on your model and compares the copies, Shared, Private and Pss.
Read CopyOnWrite.kt. Ram counts references per frame, Pte is one page-table entry, and spawn, mmap, read, exit, kill and the private frameFor are written for you.
Run the tests from the labs folder. All nine fail.
Write fork: the child gets the parent's regions and oomScoreAdj, and an entry for each of the parent's pages pointing at the same frame. Make every entry read-only on both sides and share each frame.

Write write. It has four outcomes: ZERO_FILL for a first touch, NONE for a writable entry, REUSE for a read-only entry whose frame has one reference, and COPY otherwise. Get new frames only through frameFor, and return KILLED when it gives you null.
Write smaps and oomVictim. Then read the last test: a forked snapshot that rewrites everything, as Redis does under write load.
hints: In fork, iterate over parent.pages and set pte.writable = false on the parent's own entry object before you create the child's Pte(pte.frame, writable = false).
In the COPY case, release the old frame after you have the new one. If frameFor returns null, the old frame must still belong to this entry.
PSS is sum(1.0 / ram.refCount(frame)) over the process's entries. shared counts entries whose frame has more than one reference.
Badness is rss + oomScoreAdj * ram.limit / 1000 as a Long. Use >= while you scan oldest first, so a newer process wins a tie, as in the kernel.

drill.title: Count the copies after a snapshot fork
drill.prompt: A Redis-like process holds 2 GB in 4 KB pages and forks a snapshot child. While the child runs, the parent writes to a quarter of its pages; the child only reads. Write Kotlin that prints how many pages the kernel copies, the RAM both use together, and the child's Shared, Private and Pss in MB.

answer.html: val pages = 2L * 1024 * 1024 / 4 // 524,288 pages of 4 KB val written = pages / 4 // the parent writes 131,072 of them val copies = written // one copy per page, on the parent's first write val ramMb = (pages + copies) * 4 / 1024 // 2,560 MB for the two processes // the parent's write moves the parent to the copy; the old frame is left to the child alone val childSharedMb = (pages - written) * 4 / 1024 // 1,536 MB still shared val childPrivateMb = written * 4 / 1024 // 512 MB only the child maps now val childPssMb = childSharedMb / 2 + childPrivateMb // 1,280 MB println("$copies copies, $ramMb MB, child shared $childSharedMb private $childPrivateMb pss $childPssMb") // the parent has the same split, and 1,280 + 1,280 = 2,560: PSS adds up to the RAM used

recap: fork copies the page table and marks every entry read-only on both sides. The first write to a page faults, and the kernel copies just that 4 KB page: copy-on-write.
RSS counts shared pages in full in every process; PSS splits them among the sharers, so PSS values add up to the RAM really used.

A file mapping fills pages from the page cache instead of zeros. MAP_SHARED writes reach the file; MAP_PRIVATE writes go to private copies. Clean file pages can be dropped and read again; anonymous pages can only go to swap.
Linux overcommits: mmap and fork promise memory that may never be used. Committed_AS is the total promised; vm.overcommit_memory decides whether CommitLimit is enforced.

A broken promise surfaces as a page fault with no frame. The kernel reclaims, then the OOM killer sends SIGKILL to the process with the highest badness (RSS plus oom_score_adj), inside the cgroup if memory.max was hit.
OutOfMemoryError is the JVM's heap limit and an exception you can handle. Exit 137 with oom_kill in memory.events is the kernel's limit, and nothing in the JVM runs.

explain.prompt: A teammate sees a parent process and four forked workers each showing 1 GB of RSS in ps on a machine that reports only 2 GB of RAM in use, and asks what's going on and what would happen if each worker rewrote all its data inside a 4 GB container. Explain.
explain.answer: fork doesn't copy memory. It gives each worker a page table pointing at the parent's frames, with every entry marked read-only, so all five processes map mostly the same RAM. RSS counts every page a process maps, shared or not, so each one shows the full 1 GB, but adding them up counts the shared frames five times. PSS divides each shared page among its sharers, and the five PSS values add up to roughly the 2 GB really in use: the shared data plus whatever each process has written since the fork. The copying happens later and lazily: the first write to a shared page faults, and the kernel copies that 4 KB page for the writer. If every worker rewrote all its data, each would end up with a private copy of the whole 1 GB, about 5 GB of frames in total. In a 4 GB container the charge would hit memory.max partway through, the kernel would reclaim what it could, and then the OOM killer would SIGKILL the process with the highest badness, by RSS plus oom_score_adj, and we'd see exit code 137 and oom_kill go up in memory.events.

deeper.html:
Swap changes how an OOM looks. With --memory 256m alone, Docker lets the container use as much swap again as its memory limit: inside, memory.swap.max reads 268435456 and the JVM's -XshowSettings:system reports Memory & Swap Limit: 512.00M. A hog then slows down as its oldest anonymous pages move to swap, and dies later. That's why the Try-its in this lesson pass --memory-swap 256m, which sets memory plus swap to 256 MB, so no swap at all. Many Kubernetes nodes run without swap, which behaves like the Try-its.

The cgroup has a softer limit too. memory.high makes the kernel reclaim and slow the group's allocations down once usage passes it, and it never calls the OOM killer. memory.max is the hard stop. A third file, memory.oom.group, set to 1, makes the OOM killer take every process in the group together instead of the single worst one. It was 0 in the lab box's containers.

The page-table cost of fork is real for very big processes: about 2 MB of tables per GB mapped with 4 KB pages (lesson 6). At the 1.7 ms per 512 MB measured above, a process with 30 GB touched spends about 100 ms in fork copying tables. That's one reason Java's ProcessBuilder on Linux starts children through posix_spawn, which glibc runs with CLONE_VM and CLONE_VFORK: the child borrows the parent's address space until it calls exec, and nothing is copied at all.

Finally, cow.c asks for 4 KB pages with madvise(MADV_NOHUGEPAGE), so that one write copies one 4 KB page. With transparent huge pages (lesson 6), a region can be mapped with 2 MB pages, and fault counts after fork stop being one per 4 KB, which is why the program turns them off to make the numbers readable.
